guest.bio_context: Chandra De Keyser is the co-founder of Voicera, an AI company pioneering sincerity AI technology that combines large language models with emotional intelligence. He previously founded MoodMe, one of the early innovators in emotional AI and facial analysis, which he started 14 years ago. Throughout his career he has worked across Europe, Silicon Valley and Latin America, advised startups, and led international growth initiatives. He began his career with a master's in computer science in Italy, then joined a startup in the 1980s working on an early touchscreen device from the 83rd floor of the World Trade Center.

pending_qa.q: What lessons did Chandra De Keyser learn about founding team management from his experience at MoodMe?
pending_qa.r: De Keyser says his biggest mistake at MoodMe was not firing his CTO early enough after discovering, from San Francisco, that the CTO in Italy had taken a paid side job and was not fully committed to delivering the technology. He argues that a committed founder should act fast — offering to retain the departing CTO's equity stake as recognition of early contribution while recruiting replacement engineers who could be onboarded in as little as six weeks — because allowing underperformance in a startup is damaging both to company momentum and to the motivation of high performers.

pending_qa.q: How should business leaders decide where to apply AI tools given the pace of change?
pending_qa.r: De Keyser recommends that leaders identify their specific execution bottlenecks first — whether in product development, marketing, or another function — and then test focused AI tools against those bottlenecks rather than trying to follow every development. He cites examples from his own company: using Cursor and Claude Code to potentially double or quadruple engineering speed, and a new CMO candidate who rebuilt the Voicera website using Lovable as part of the interview process in just a couple of hours.

pending_qa.q: What qualities does Chandra De Keyser believe separate founders who survive from those who fail?
pending_qa.r: De Keyser highlights two qualities above all: the ability to build and maintain the right team — including the willingness to let go of people quickly when their performance or commitment declines — and persistence through early failures before finding product-market fit. He references the founding stories of Airbnb and Twitch as examples of companies that nearly gave up before finding the formula, and warns that even well-funded companies can enter paralysis when confronted with the speed of AI development.
